details:
**"Jupiter" Symphony (Symphony No. 41 in C major)**
Mozart's 41st and final symphony, nicknamed after the Roman king of the gods. Its finale opens with the whole-note theme "C, D, F, E" and ends in a famous five-voice fugato that combines all of the movement's themes at once.

**"Great" and "Little" G minor symphonies**
Symphony No. 40 ("Great" G minor) and Symphony No. 25 ("Little" G minor) are Mozart's only two minor-key symphonies. No. 40, his penultimate symphony, opens with a bar of accompaniment from divided violas before the violins' sighing "E-flat, D, D" figure, and Mozart later revised it to add two clarinet parts.

**Requiem in D minor (K. 626)**
Mozart's final composition, a mass for the dead secretly commissioned by Count Franz von Walsegg. Mozart died in 1791 having written only the first eight or so bars of the "Lacrimosa," and his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, writing the Sanctus and Agnus Dei; the final "Lux aeterna" reuses the music of the opening two sections.

**"Tuba mirum"**
A section of the Requiem's sequence in which a solo trombone outlines a descending B-flat major triad that the bass soloist then imitates. Other Requiem clues include the opening bassoon and basset horn theme modeled on Handel's Funeral Anthem for Queen Caroline, the Kyrie double fugue quoting Handel's "And with his stripes we are healed," and the sighing 12/8 Larghetto "Lacrimosa" that follows the "Confutatis."

**The Magic Flute (Die Zauberflöte)**
Mozart's 1791 German-language singspiel. The Queen of the Night sings the coloratura aria "Der Hölle Rache," with its repeated high F6 notes, ordering her daughter Pamina to murder the sorcerer Sarastro.

**"Rondo alla Turca" (Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major, K. 331)**
The A minor finale of this sonata imitates the percussion-heavy music of Turkish Janissary bands. The sonata unusually skips sonata form in its first movement, which is a set of variations on a 6/8 siciliana-like theme marked "Andante grazioso"; Max Reger wrote "Variations and Fugue" on that theme.

**Sonata facile (Piano Sonata No. 16 in C major, K. 545)**
A simple piano sonata that Mozart labeled "for beginners," also called "semplice." It begins with an ascending C major triad melody over a rocking Alberti bass and is a staple for piano students.

**Clarinet Concerto in A major (K. 622)**
One of Mozart's last works, written for clarinetist Anton Stadler and originally intended for the lower-ranged basset clarinet. Mozart also featured the clarinet alongside viola and piano in the "Kegelstatt" Trio, named for a bowling alley where skittles are played.

**Horn concertos for Joseph Leutgeb**
Mozart wrote four horn concertos for his friend Leutgeb, a skilled natural horn player. The manuscripts are written in multicolored ink and include joking, mocking comments aimed at the soloist.

**Eine kleine Nachtmusik (Serenade No. 13 in G major, K. 525)**
A serenade for strings whose title translates to "A Little Night Music." It opens with a rising arpeggiated figure known as a Mannheim rocket.

**Così fan tutte**
An opera in which Ferrando and Guglielmo, egged on by the cynical Don Alfonso, bet on whether their fiancées Fiordiligi and Dorabella will stay faithful, and test them by returning in disguise. It includes the trio "Soave sia il vento," wishing the departing men gentle winds, and Ferrando's aria "Un'aura amorosa."

**"Jeunehomme" and "Coronation" piano concertos**
Two of Mozart's 27 piano concertos. The "Jeunehomme" (No. 9, E-flat major) was long thought to be for an unnamed young woman but was actually written for Victoire Jenamy, and its rondo finale is interrupted by a slow minuet; the "Coronation" (No. 26) was played around Leopold II's 1790 coronation and has a left-hand piano part Mozart left largely unwritten.

**Don Giovanni and The Marriage of Figaro**
Two Mozart operas with libretti by Lorenzo Da Ponte. In Don Giovanni, the unrepentant title seducer is dragged to hell by the statue of the Commendatore, and Don Ottavio swears vengeance in "Il mio tesoro"; in Figaro, the title servant marries Susanna after thwarting Count Almaviva, and sings "Non più andrai."

**Gran Partita (Serenade No. 10, K. 361)**
A seven-movement serenade scored for twelve wind instruments and double bass. It is one of several prominent Mozart wind works, alongside his B-flat major bassoon concerto, C major oboe concerto, and the Concerto for Flute and Harp commissioned by the Duke of Guînes.

**Child prodigy from Salzburg**
Mozart was born in Salzburg and toured Europe as a child with his father Leopold and his older sister Nannerl, whose playing he emulated when learning keyboard. He wrote his first symphony at about eight years old.
